issues.legal_issue: A statutory provision is not unconstitutionally vague merely because its drafting has caused interpretive difficulty when it has been authoritatively construed and applied.
material_facts: The challenge alleged that the provision governing a Hindu woman's property rights was vague and uncertain.

An earlier Supreme Court decision had criticized the provision's drafting but had construed and applied it, holding that property allotted to a woman in lieu of maintenance became her absolute property.
The Court found the woman's position in this case to be no different from that considered in the earlier decision.
issues.conclusion: The vagueness challenge failed; the provision was capable of construction and implementation, and the failure to amend it did not prevent its application.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 was construed and applied in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi. Although that decision criticized the provision's drafting and suggested recasting it to avoid litigation, it did not hold the provision incapable of construction or application; its construction resolved the relevant doubt.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party seeks a ruling that a statutory provision is constitutionally invalid.
predicates.vagueness_challenge: The party claims that the provision is too uncertain to be applied.
predicates.prior_authoritative_application: A prior authoritative decision construed and applied the provision despite identifying difficulties in its drafting.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge rests on vagueness and a prior authoritative decision has construed and applied the provision, the vagueness challenge is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A sex-specific protective measure for women is not unconstitutional discrimination when the constitutional framework permits special provisions for women and the measure addresses their disadvantage.
material_facts: The petitioner argued that the provision benefited Hindu women on the ground of sex and prejudiced Hindu men.
The provision was enacted to improve the position of Hindu women whose inherited property interests had been subject to restrictions under Hindu law.
The Constitution expressly permits special provisions for women.
issues.conclusion: The sex-discrimination challenge failed because the provision was a permissible special measure for the benefit of women.
issues.legal_principle: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on specified grounds, including sex, but Article 15(3) permits the State to make special provisions for women and children. The Court held that Article 15(3) protected the beneficial provision enacted for Hindu women.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and sex_specific_classification and protective_measure_addresses_disadvantage and constitution_authorizes_special_provisions

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party seeks a ruling that a statutory provision is constitutionally invalid.
predicates.sex_specific_classification: The challenged measure differentiates on the basis of sex and benefits women.
predicates.protective_measure_addresses_disadvantag: The measure is intended to remedy a disadvantage experienced by women.
predicates.constitution_authorizes_special_provisio: The governing constitutional framework expressly permits special protective provisions for women.

issues.definition: A constitutional equality challenge to a sex-specific measure is rejected when the measure addresses women's disadvantage and the constitutional framework authorizes special provisions for women.

issues.legal_issue: A limited interest in property given to a woman in lieu of her pre-existing maintenance right becomes absolute when the statutory enlargement of women's property rights applies.
material_facts: A widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance from her husband's estate.
Under a compromise decree, she retained a share of the estate in lieu of maintenance, subject to the agreement that another person would receive possession after her death.
She possessed the share when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
She later bequeathed the share, and the petitioner conceded that the will was genuine and valid.
issues.conclusion: The widow's interest became absolute under Section 14(1), so the petitioner could not recover the property after her death on the basis of the compromise decree's restriction; the special leave petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as applied in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, property allotted to a Hindu woman in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance became her absolute property despite a restriction in the instrument granting it.

predicates.civil_claim_for_recovery_after_widow_dea: A civil proceeding seeks recovery of property after the death of a woman who had held it.
predicates.property_given_in_lieu_of_preexisting_ma: The woman received the property in recognition or satisfaction of a maintenance right she already had.
predicates.grant_restricted_the_woman_to_a_limited_: The instrument granting the property purported to limit her interest or provide for another person's possession after her death.
predicates.woman_held_property_when_rights_reform_t: The woman possessed the property when the legal reform enlarging women's property rights took effect.

issues.definition: When a woman holds property at the time of the relevant reform after receiving it for a pre-existing maintenance right, a restriction in the grant does not prevent her limited interest from becoming absolute.
